options.denominator: None; counts of people killed in crashes
options.reason: Side-by-side counts make the absolute annual difference easy to compare.
options.answer: Motorist deaths exceeded cyclist deaths every year; the largest gap was 134 versus 19 in 2021, while the smallest was 82 versus 31 in 2019.
options.interpretation: This framing answers how many motorist and cyclist deaths were recorded in each year and makes their absolute differences visible. Counts are a direct and defensible measure of annual fatality burden, but they do not express the gap relative to cyclist deaths or emphasize the shape of the trends.

options.denominator: None; counts of people killed in crashes
options.reason: Lines make the direction and timing of year-to-year changes easy to follow.
options.answer: Motorist deaths were higher in every year, peaking at 139 in 2020 and falling to 81 in 2025, while cyclist deaths peaked at 31 in 2019 and 2023.
options.interpretation: This framing answers how the two annual death counts changed over time, showing a motorist peak in 2020 and cyclist peaks in 2019 and 2023. A line chart is defensible for ordered yearly observations and makes timing and direction salient, but the separation between series can make the proportional comparison less clear.

options.denominator: Cyclist deaths in the same calendar year
options.chart_type: Line chart of annual ratios with a 1:1 reference line
options.reason: The ratio shows the relative scale of motorist deaths compared with cyclist deaths each year.
options.answer: Motorist deaths ranged from 2.6 times cyclist deaths in 2019 to 10.0 times in 2013; the ratio was 3.5 in 2025.
options.interpretation: This framing answers how many motorist deaths there were for each cyclist death in a given year, with the 1:1 line indicating equal counts. A ratio is a defensible way to compare relative scale despite the groups' different counts, but it does not show the absolute number of deaths by group on its own.
